newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. calls for Iraq oil deal renewal, U.S. concurs.
newsitem.headline: U.N. calls for Iraq oil deal renewal, U.S. concurs.

text.p: United Nations Secretary General Kofi Annan has recommended that Security Council members extend the Iraqi "oil-for-food" accord for another six months at the current $2 billion ceiling, according to a draft report obtained by Reuters on Monday.
In Washington, a source familiar with the administration's decision said on Monday that the United State's "will be looking favorably toward the rollover."

The U.S. has been the only one of the U.N. Security Council members to express doubts that the deal would be renewed. Indeed, State Department spokesman John Dinger told reporters Monday: "We will study the issue closely and make our determination closer to the time of renewal."

The current deal, a humanitarian exception to the broader economic sanctions in place since Iraq's invasion of Kuwait in 1990, expires on June 7. Under its terms, Baghdad is allowed to use the bulk of the proceeds to buy food, medicines and other necessities to be distributed to ordinary Iraqis who have been suffering under the sanctions regime.

The 15 Security Council members are expected to receive Annan's final report on Tuesday, a U.N. spokesman said. Before the oil deal can be renewed, the Security Council must agree on another resolution to extend the terms.

In Annan's draft report he says: "In light of the experience gained in the implementation of the program in the past six months and bearing in mind the continuing humanitarian crisis in Iraq, I recommend the renewal of the program for a further period of six months."

Baghdad and some of its supporters on the Security Council, particularly Russia, have complained about the slowness of the U.N. approval process for humanitarian goods and blamed Washington for delays.
Annan's report also criticizes persistent delays in processing food and other applications.

"It is my sincere hope that this situation can soon be remedied with the cooperation of all concerned so as to ensure, should the Council decide to extend the program, that steps are taken to include in the distribution plan the necessary provisions to satisfy unmet needs of an urgent nature," the draft report said.
Annan states that as of May 28 1997, the United Nations Treasury had processed letters of credit for approximately $2.11 billion worth of petroleum.

Proceeds amounting to just under $1.75 billion were deposited into the U.N.-Iraq Account at the Banque Nationale de Paris. Letters of credit amounting to $465.9 million have been issued by BNP on behalf of the U.N. for the payment of humanitarian supplies destined for the whole of Iraq.

"As of May 30, 630 applications for exports of humanitarian supplies to Iraq had been received by the ... (sanctions committee). Of the 574 circulated to the committee, 331 were approved, 191 placed on hold, 14 blocked, 24 cancelled and 38 are pending under the "no objection" procedure or awaiting clarification," Annan's report said.

On the oil sales side, the report said that the second 90-day period had seen 65 loadings totalling 67.9 million barrels at an estimated value of $1.116 billion. Three of these liftings are delayed loadings from the first 90 days.

"In May, market prices jumped to such a level that total revenue generated by delivering the remaining contract volumes for the second 90-day period would be somewhat in excess of the 180-day objective of $2.14 billion...if prevailing prices remain unchanged," the report said.
On May 23, the sanctions committee reached an understanding for dealing with possible excess revenues over the 180-day objective, the report said.

Though the report did not go into detail on this point, the meeting of the U.N. Sanctions Committee on Iraq agreed to allow oil sales which might produce revenue above the allowed level but that the proceeds would be frozen pending a new resolution to extend the deal.
Despite Washington's doubts, analysts said it makes sense for the administration to renew the deal on current terms.
"This is oil politics," said Mohammed Abduljabbar, a cunsultant at The Petroleum Finance Co in Washington.

To disrupt or stop the deal would cause an inflationary surge in oil prices and allowing an increase could cause concern for oil-producing U.S. allies such as Saudi Arabia. "This level is comfortable. If you change it you upset oil producers like Saudi Arabia, U.S. oil companies, the market, everybody," said Abduljabbar.
